description: Vega 49 is a Vancouver-based solo team exploring "Filed Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data". The project aims to turn NASA Earth observations, soil information, crop characteristics, and weather data into an intuitive tool for exploring stable crop rotation strategies and visualize their potential impacts on soil health, water availability, and environmental conditions.
summary:
What we built:
Stardew Earth turns a real farm into a digital twin you can explore in 3D and 2D. It then forecasts how climate change will reshape that farm over 10 years.

How it meets the challenge:
- NASA data: replays real NASA POWER weather and storms on the farm model.
- Three rotations: compares at least three crop rotations, including the existing one.
- Explained for farmers: each rotation shows why, evidence, benefits, gaps and risks, in plain language.
- Honest numbers: every figure shows its unit and whether it was measured, modeled or assumed. It supports, and does not replace, local agronomic expertise.

Why it matters:
Rotation choices usually rest on rules of thumb that ignore the shape of a specific field. A low corner floods and a slope erodes. Stardew Earth lets farmers see their own land adapt to a changing climate before committing a season.
details:
Project Details

Farming is a one-shot game. You pick a rotation in spring, you find out in fall, and the climate keeps moving the goalposts. Nobody hands you a "what if" button. So we built one.

What it does

Stardew Earth turns a real farm into a digital twin you can explore in 3D and 2D, then forecasts what the next ten years do to it. Drag the timeline from 2026 to 2035 and the fields change as real NASA POWER weather and storms replay over them. Flip to "Next 12 months" for a month-by-month outlook with ranges that widen the further out you look.

Then it gets competitive. Three crop rotations, including the one the farm already uses, go head to head. Each one comes with why it wins or loses, the evidence, the benefits, the risks and the information gaps. Built-in explainers cover the jargon (NDVI, evapotranspiration, erosion, ponding) so you don't need an agronomy degree.

You can also:

- Ask Gus, an in-app farm assistant, about whatever you're looking at.

- Plan your own rotations in the rotation planner.

- Arrange the screen your way. Every panel is a window you can drag, resize, minimise or hide, and the layout is remembered.

Why it's different

- It's honest. Every number shows its units anmodeled or assumed. Forecasts carry p10 to p90ranges. Curated sites wear a "Pre-built" badge, and synthetic fixture data is labelled as such. Prices come from the

farmer, never from us.

- It's repeatable. Same inputs give the same outputs. There's an offline mode that serves only pre-built data, so the

demo can't be broken by bad Wi-Fi.

- It respects the experts. The tool supports, and does not replace, local agronomic expertise.

How we built it

- Front end: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, react-three-fiber, MapLibre GL, Framer Motion, Zustand, Recharts.

- Back end: Python 3.11, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy Pillow, httpx.

- Data: NASA POWER for weather, plus satellite vegetation imagery for field health.

- Process: one shared OpenAPI contract with fiback end could be built in parallel. Tested with Vitest, pytest and Playwright.

Challenges we ran into

- Making a forecast you can trust. It's easy to make numbers look confident. It's harder to make them admit what they don't know. We spent real time on ranges, la instead of pretty guesses.

- A timeline that sits still. Scrubbing changed the width of the year and date text, so everything next to it jiggled. We fixed it with fixed-width tabular numeraling moves by even a pixel across every month.

- A crowded screen. Maps, timelines, drawers and an assistant all fight for space. We built a small window manager from scratch, with edge resizing, a rubber-band bt lost off-screen, and saved layouts.

What we're proud of

- It's a decision tool, not a weather widget.

- Pre-built sites for UBC Farm and KPU Langley work end to end.

- Honest labelling is built into every screen the end.

What's next

Drone and video capture are on the roadmap, an working in this version. We also want morefarms, more crops, and real farmer feedback on whether the rotation advice matches what they see in their fields.
